Chapter 2 Project description This webbook contains all the code used for data analysis in our study on the hologenomic ecology of wild possums. We integrate host genomic variation with shotgun metagenomic profiles of the gut microbiome to examine how environment and diet are associated with microbial composition, diversity, and function. We sampled free-ranging possums across multiple sites and environment types (e.g., contrasting habitat/land-use categories), recorded basic covariates (such as sex and body measurements), and generated both host and microbial DNA data from faecal material. Rather than imposing laboratory treatments, this study leverages natural ecological variation to test whether differences among environment types and related ecological factors are linked to shifts in the gut microbiome and to host genetic backgrounds. Analytically, the webbook documents the complete workflow: data import and quality control; mapping and recovery metrics; taxonomic and functional summaries; diversity analyses (Hill numbers) and community structure tests; and differential abundance comparisons across environment types and other covariates. Where relevant, we also relate microbial features (e.g., dominant taxa, MAGs, and pathway profiles) to host genomic patterns to explore potential hologenomic links between ecology, microbiota, and host variation. Together, these analyses provide a reproducible, end-to-end account of how we interrogate possum hologenomes to understand microbiome–environment–host relationships in the wild. 2.1 Prepare the R environment 2.1.1 Environment To reproduce all the analyses locally, clone this repository in your computer using: RStudio > New Project > Version Control > Git And indicating the following git repository: ##included later Once the R project has been created, follow the instructions and code chunks shown in this webbook. 2.1.2 Libraries The following R packages are required for the data analysis. # Base library(dplyr) library(forcats) library(janitor) library(purrr) library(readr) library(readxl) library(rlang) library(stringr) library(tibble) library(tidyr) library(xml2) # for tree handling library(ape) library(phytools) # for statistics library(ANCOMBC) library(Hmsc) library(Rtsne) library(broom.mixed) library(distillR) library(emmeans) library(geiger) library(hilldiv2) library(lme4) library(nlme) library(phyloseq) library(spaa) library(vegan) library(pairwiseAdonis) # map visualisation library(exactextractr) library(geodata) library(rnaturalearth) library(rnaturalearthdata) library(sf) library(terra) # other library(corrplot) library(cowplot) library(devtools) library(GGally) library(ggnewscale) library(ggplot2) library(ggpubr) library(ggrepel) library(ggh4x) library(ggtree) library(ggtreeExtra) library(gridExtra) library(knitr) library(patchwork) library(pheatmap) library(R.utils) library(RColorBrewer) library(rairtable) library(tinytable) library(UpSetR) library(ComplexUpset) # for web/API interactions library(httr) library(jsonlite)

Chapter 3 Prepare data We load pipeline outputs and metadata, harmonise identifiers, and derive working objects used downstream: coverage-filtered counts, genome lengths and phylogeny, genome annotations (via Airtable), colour palettes, and GIFT-based functional tables. Everything is wrapped as a single RData for reuse. 3.1 Load data Load the original data files outputted by the bioinformatic pipeline. 3.1.1 Sample metadata Note: Load sample metadata from the merged metadata file. The first column is renamed to “sample” to ensure consistent naming across the analysis. sample_metadata <- read_tsv("data/merged_metadata.tsv") %>% rename(sample=1) 3.2 load_read_counts Note: Load read count data from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome” and select only columns corresponding to samples present in the metadata. This ensures data consistency between counts and metadata. read_counts <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_counts.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(one_of(c("genome",sample_metadata$sample))) # Select specific columns from the data 3.3 load_genome_metadata Note: Load genome metadata (MAG information) from the compressed TSV file. Rename “mag_size” to “length” for consistency. Filter to only include genomes present in the read counts data and arrange them in the same order as read_counts to ensure alignment across datasets. genome_metadata <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_mag_info.tsv.gz") %>% rename(length=mag_size)%>% semi_join(., read_counts, by = "genome") %>% arrange(match(genome,read_counts$genome)) 3.4 Genome base hits Note: Load genome coverage data (base hits) from the compressed TSV file. Rename the first column to “genome”, select only columns for samples in metadata, filter to genomes present in genome_metadata, and arrange in the same order as read_counts. This coverage data is used to filter low-coverage genomes. genome_coverage <- read_tsv("data/DMB0167_coverage.tsv.gz") %>% rename(genome=1) %>% select(one_of(c("genome",sample_metadata$sample)))%>% # Select specific columns from the data semi_join(., genome_metadata, by = "genome")%>% arrange(match(genome, read_counts$genome)) 3.5 Genome tree Note: Load the phylogenetic tree of genomes from the compressed Newick file. Remove single quotes from tip labels (MAG names) and prune the tree to only include tips corresponding to genomes in the metadata. This ensures the tree matches the genomes used in downstream analyses. genome_tree <- read_tree("data/DMB0167.tree.gz") genome_tree$tip.label <- str_replace_all(genome_tree$tip.label,"'", "") #remove single quotes in MAG names genome_tree <- keep.tip(genome_tree, tip=genome_metadata$genome) # keep only MAG tips 3.6 Genome annotations Note: Download genome annotation files from ERDA using Airtable metadata. This chunk connects to Airtable, retrieves annotation URLs for MAGs with genes, downloads all annotation tables, and combines them into a single compressed file. This only needs to be run once to generate the genome_annotations table. Note that the Airtable connection requires a personal access token. airtable("MAGs", "appWbHBNLE6iAsMRV") %>% #get base ID from Airtable browser URL read_airtable(., fields = c("ID","mag_name","number_genes","anno_url"), id_to_col = TRUE) %>% #get 3 columns from MAGs table filter(mag_name %in% paste0(genome_metadata$genome,".fa")) %>% #filter by MAG name filter(number_genes > 0) %>% #genes need to exist select(anno_url) %>% #list MAG annotation urls pull() %>% read_tsv() %>% #load all tables rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) %>% #rename first 3 columns write_tsv(file="data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") #write to overall compressed file Note: Load the pre-generated genome annotations table from the compressed file. Rename the first three columns to “gene”, “genome”, and “contig” for consistency. This annotation data is used for functional analysis using the GIFT framework. genome_annotations <- read_tsv("data/genome_annotations.tsv.xz") %>% rename(gene=1, genome=2, contig=3) 3.7 Filter reads by coverage Note: Filter read counts based on genome coverage. Set minimum coverage threshold (0.3) and create a binary mask where genomes with coverage above the threshold are kept (1) and below are excluded (0). Multiply read counts by this mask to zero out reads from low-coverage genomes, ensuring only high-quality genome assignments are retained. min_coverage=0.3 read_counts_filt <- genome_coverage %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ ifelse(. > min_coverage, 1, 0))) %>% # Add or modify columns in the dataset mutate(across(-1, ~ . * read_counts[[cur_column()]])) # Add or modify columns in the dataset 3.8 Transform reads into genome counts Note: Transform raw read counts into normalized genome counts by dividing by genome length (scaled by read length). This accounts for the fact that longer genomes will naturally have more reads mapped to them, normalizing counts to represent relative abundance rather than absolute read numbers. readlength=150 genome_counts <- read_counts %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . / (genome_metadata$length / readlength) )) # Add or modify columns in the dataset Note: Transform filtered read counts (after coverage filtering) into normalized genome counts using the same length normalization approach. This creates the filtered genome count matrix used in downstream analyses, excluding low-coverage genomes. readlength=150 genome_counts_filt <- read_counts_filt %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ . / (genome_metadata$length / readlength) )) # Add or modify columns in the dataset 3.8.1 Distill annotations into GIFTs Note: Convert genome annotations into GIFT (Genome-Inferred Functional Traits) format using the distillR package. This aggregates gene-level annotations into functional trait profiles for each genome, which are used for community-level functional analysis. The function processes annotations from columns 9, 10, and 19 of the annotation table. genome_gifts <- distill(genome_annotations,GIFT_db,genomecol=2,annotcol=c(9,10,19), verbosity=F) 3.9 Prepare color scheme Note: Load phylum-level color scheme from the EHI taxonomy color repository. Join with genome metadata to get colors for phyla present in the dataset, arrange to match the tree tip order, and create a named vector mapping phylum names to colors. This ensures consistent color coding across all visualizations. phylum_colors <- read_tsv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/earthhologenome/EHI_taxonomy_colour/main/ehi_phylum_colors.tsv") %>% right_join(genome_metadata, by=join_by(phylum == phylum)) %>% arrange(match(genome, genome_tree$tip.label)) %>% select(phylum, colors) %>% unique() %>% arrange(phylum) %>% pull(colors, name=phylum) Note: Classify samples into geographic regions (Tasmania vs Australia) based on latitude and longitude coordinates. Samples within the specified geographic bounds are classified as “Tasmania”, all others as “Australia”. This creates a categorical variable for geographic analysis. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% mutate( island = case_when( latitude < -38 & latitude > -45 & longitude > 140 & longitude < 150 ~ "Tasmania", TRUE ~ "Australia" ) ) 3.10 Wrap working objects Note: Save all processed data objects into a single RData file for efficient loading in downstream analyses. This includes sample metadata, genome metadata, read counts, normalized genome counts (both filtered and unfiltered), phylogenetic tree, GIFT functional annotations, and color schemes. All subsequent chapters load this single file to access the prepared data. save(sample_metadata, genome_metadata, read_counts, genome_counts, genome_counts_filt, genome_tree, genome_gifts, phylum_colors, file = "data/data.Rdata")

Chapter 4 Data statistics Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, genome counts, and other prepared datasets from the RData file created in the data preparation chapter. load("data/data.Rdata") #Visualisation of geographical location of samples and their respectiv envirotypes 4.1 Helper Functions Note: Define helper function to filter and aggregate geographic data by environment variable. This eliminates code duplication and allows reuse for both broad and local environment classifications. 4.2 Filter Data Note: Filter sample metadata by geographic boundaries to create datasets for full Australia/Tasmania region and Tasmania-only region. Aggregate sample counts per location and broad environment type to prepare data for mapping visualization. # Filter by broad environment broad_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "broad_environment") full_possums <- broad_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- broad_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- broad_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.3 Load Map Note: Load Australia country boundary data from Natural Earth dataset to use as the base map for geographic visualizations. This provides the geographic context for plotting sample locations. # Load world map australia_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>% filter(admin == "Australia") 4.4 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by broad environment type. The first plot shows the full dataset across Australia, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. Point sizes represent the number of samples per location. Combine both plots and save to PDF for publication. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania (with entire landmass and cleaned longitude labels) map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + # Base map geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = broad_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + # Full Tasmania view theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", color = "Environment Type", size = "Count") + theme(legend.position = "right", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold")) combined_plot <- (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(guides = "collect", widths = c(1, 1.2)) combined_plot # ---- SAVE TO PDF ---- ggsave( filename = "Sample _maps.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 8, # adjust for your needs height = 4, # adjust for your needs units = "in", device = cairo_pdf # nice for text/embedding fonts ) Note: Filter sample metadata again, this time grouping by local_environment instead of broad_environment. This creates alternative datasets for mapping with more detailed environment classifications. Aggregate sample counts per location and local environment type. # Filter by local environment local_env_data <- filter_geographic_data(sample_metadata, "local_environment") full_possums <- local_env_data$full_possums tasmania_possums <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums full_possums_count <- local_env_data$full_possums_count tasmania_possums_count <- local_env_data$tasmania_possums_count 4.5 Plot Possum Locations Note: Create two side-by-side map visualizations showing sample locations colored by local environment type using a viridis color scale. The first plot shows the full dataset, while the second plot zooms into Tasmania. This provides a more detailed view of environmental classifications compared to the broad environment maps. # Count total possums total_full <- sum(full_possums_count$count) total_tasmania <- sum(tasmania_possums_count$count) # Plot 1: Full Dataset (Including Border Data) map_plot_full <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = full_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Full Dataset (", total_full, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), legend.position = "none" ) # Plot 2: Zoomed-in Tasmania map_plot_zoomed <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = australia_map, fill = "lightgray", color = "black") + geom_point(data = tasmania_possums_count, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = local_environment, size = count), alpha = 0.8) + coord_sf(xlim = c(143, 149), ylim = c(-44, -39)) + scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Environment Type", option = "D") + theme_minimal() + labs(title = paste("PD - Tasmania (", total_tasmania, ")"), x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") + theme( plot.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none" ) # Combine the plots side by side (map_plot_full + map_plot_zoomed) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) Note: Create a custom legend plot showing all local environment types with their average sample counts. Chapter 7 Alpha diversity We quantify within-sample diversity using Hill numbers: richness (q0), neutral/abundance-weighted (q1), phylogenetic (q1 + tree), and functional (q1 + traits), and compare these across environments and sex. 7.1 microbiota Note: Load all required data objects including genome counts, metadata, and color schemes. Set factor levels for broad_environment variable to ensure consistent ordering. load("data/data.Rdata") treatment_colors <- c("#f56042","#429ef5", "#42f58d", "#b142f5", "#FFA500") sample_metadata$broad_environment <- factor(sample_metadata$broad_environment, levels=c("1000198 - Mixed forest", "1000221 - Temperate woodland", "1000218 - Xeric shrubland", "1000215 - Temperate shrubland", "1000245 - Cropland")) Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 and filter genome counts to only include valid samples. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") valid_samples <- sample_metadata$sample genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% dplyr::select(genome, tidyselect::any_of(valid_samples)) Note: Prune the phylogenetic tree to match genomes present in the filtered count data. Identifies genomes that exist in both the count data and the tree, then removes tree tips that don’t have corresponding count data. # 1) Figure out the common labels otus <- genome_counts_filt$genome tips <- genome_tree$tip.label common <- intersect(tips, otus) # 2) Prune the tree to only those tips genome_tree_pruned <- drop.tip(genome_tree, setdiff(tips, common)) 7.1.1 Hill numbers Richness of microbiotic species in samples Note: Calculate four types of Hill number diversity metrics for each sample: richness (q=0, species count unweighted by abundance), neutral (q=1, Shannon diversity abundance-weighted), phylogenetic (q=1 + tree, incorporates phylogenetic relationships), and functional (q=1 + traits, incorporates functional trait distances). Then merge all metrics into a single alpha_div dataframe. # Calculate Hill numbers richness <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 0) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(richness = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") neutral <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(neutral = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") phylogenetic <- genome_counts_filt %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, tree = genome_tree_pruned) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(phylogenetic = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") # Aggregate basal GIFT into elements dist <- genome_gifts %>% to.elements(., GIFT_db) %>% traits2dist(., method = "gower") functional <- genome_counts_filt %>% filter(genome %in% rownames(dist)) %>% column_to_rownames(var = "genome") %>% dplyr::select(where(~ !all(. == 0))) %>% hilldiv(., q = 1, dist = dist) %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(functional = 1) %>% rownames_to_column(var = "sample") %>% mutate(functional = if_else(is.nan(functional), 1, functional)) # Merge all metrics alpha_div <- richness %>% full_join(neutral, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(phylogenetic, by = join_by(sample == sample)) %>% full_join(functional, by = join_by(sample == sample)) Note: Create a summary statistics table showing mean ± SD for each alpha diversity metric. Chapter 11 environmental permanova We test whether environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2 of land-cover) relates to microbiome β-diversity (Bray–Curtis), and visualise relationships (e.g., NMDS axes vs. Hill metrics) and distance-matrix structure. 11.1 Load data Note: Load all required data objects including sample metadata, beta diversity matrices, and Hill diversity metrics from the RData files created in previous chapters. 11.2 Data preparation Note: Filter out sample EHI01340 from the metadata and Hill diversity data. This sample was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% dplyr::filter(sample != "EHI01340") hill_long <- hill_long %>% dplyr::filter(id != "EHI01340") Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 11.3 Helper functions Note: Helper function to align metadata with distance matrices. This eliminates code duplication when aligning metadata for multiple distance matrices. Defined early as it’s needed by multiple analysis sections. Note: Optimized helper function that accepts pre-calculated NMDS object instead of recalculating. This eliminates redundant NMDS calculations when creating multiple plots. 11.4 Ordination analysis Note: Extract distance matrices from beta diversity objects for use in ordination analyses. These matrices represent Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between samples at different diversity orders. Note: Calculate all NMDS ordinations once upfront. These are expensive operations (trymax = 500 iterations each) and were previously calculated redundantly 3+ times. This optimization saves significant computation time. Note: Align metadata with each distance matrix using the helper function. This ensures proper sample order matching for ordination and visualization. 11.5 Grouping variables Note: Create grouping variables for environmental Hill diversity metrics. Calculate medians once to avoid redundant calculations. Split into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) and median-based groups (Low, High) for visualization and statistical testing. Note: Verify the grouping variables were created correctly by displaying frequency tables. This ensures balanced group sizes for downstream analyses. 11.10 Visualization Associations between environmental α-diversity (Hill h0/h1/h2) and microbiome ordination (NMDS1/2), with fitted vectors and a subset heatmap of Bray–Curtis distances. Note: Create combined scatterplots showing relationships between all environmental Hill diversity metrics and NMDS ordination axes. This provides a comprehensive view of how environmental diversity relates to microbiome β-diversity ordination. Uses loess smoothing instead of linear regression, which is more appropriate for potentially non-linear relationships. Note: Fit environmental Hill diversity vectors (h0, h1, h2) onto the q0 NMDS ordination using envfit. This tests the correlation between environmental variables and ordination axes, displaying significant vectors as arrows on the ordination plot. Improved visualization using ggplot2 for consistency with other plots. Note: Create an improved heatmap visualization of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix with sample grouping information. This shows clustering patterns in microbiome β-diversity and how they relate to environmental Hill diversity groups. Uses all samples (or a representative subset if too large) with grouping annotations. #abundance analysis of micrb community in diffrent enviroment diversitys This chapter analyzes differential abundance of microbial genomes between samples with low and high environmental diversity (Hill diversity metrics h0, h1, h2). We use ANCOM-BC2 to identify significantly differentially abundant genomes and visualize results with barplots and volcano plots. 11.11 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. Filter out sample EHI01340 which was removed because it could not be mapped to MAGs, ensuring consistency across downstream analyses. Note: Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format, creating separate columns for each Hill diversity metric (env_hill_h0, env_hill_h1, env_hill_h2). Join with sample metadata to create a combined metadata object for downstream analyses. 11.12 Data preparation Note: Create grouping variables for each Hill diversity metric (q0, q1, q2). Split samples into tertiles (Low, Mid, High) based on environmental Hill diversity, then filter to keep only Low and High groups for two-group comparisons. For each q value, create filtered metadata and genome count matrices containing only samples in Low/High groups and genomes present in at least one sample. n filtered_inputs = 3 q=0 nLow=30 nHigh=20 genomes=1750 q=1 nLow=25 nHigh=17 genomes=1522 q=2 nLow=24 nHigh=17 genomes=1514 11.13 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. This is important for ANCOM-BC2 analysis as structural zeros can be handled explicitly. For each q value, calculate which genomes are structurally absent in Low vs High groups and compute group means for genomes that are present in only one group. Note: Create UpSet plot using UpSetR to visualize the intersection of genomes present in Low and High environmental diversity groups. The plot shows unique genomes in each group and shared genomes, with colors indicating group membership. 11.14 Differential abundance analysis 11.14.1 Build phyloseq objects Note: Create phyloseq objects for each q value (q0, q1, q2) containing OTU table (genome counts), taxonomy table, and sample metadata. Counts are kept as integers with zeros allowed, as ANCOM-BC2 can handle zeros without requiring pseudocounts. Sample metadata includes the grouping variable (Low/High) for each Hill diversity metric. 11.14.2 Run ANCOM-BC2 analysis Note: Perform ANCOM-BC2 differential abundance testing for each q value, comparing Low vs High environmental diversity groups. The analysis uses structural zero modeling (struc_zero=TRUE) to properly handle genomes absent in one group. Version-adaptive code handles differences between ANCOMBC package versions. Results include log fold-changes, p-values, and adjusted p-values for each genome. 11.14.3 Visualize differential abundance results Note: Extract significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05) from ANCOM-BC2 results and create visualizations. Barplots show log2 fold-changes for significant genomes, ordered by effect size and colored by phylum. Volcano plots show all tested genomes with log2 fold-change on x-axis and -log10(p-value) on y-axis, highlighting significant hits. Both visualizations are created for each q value (q0, q1, q2). Note: Alternative barplot visualization using genome identifiers instead of taxon names. This provides a different view of the same differential abundance results, useful for identifying specific genomes of interest. 11.15 Alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros Note: Run an alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with additional structural zero handling parameters. This analysis uses a random effects model (rand_formula=“~1”) and different parameter settings including Holm p-value adjustment, pseudo-sensitivity analysis, and explicit structural zero detection. This provides a complementary view to the main analysis and may identify additional differentially abundant genomes. Note: Extract and clean results from the alternative ANCOM-BC2 analysis with structural zeros. Filter for significantly differentially abundant genomes (p < 0.05), join with taxonomy information, and create cleaned tables ready for visualization or further analysis. Results are organized by log fold-change for easy interpretation. 11.16 Load data Note: Load sample metadata, genome count data, and Hill diversity metrics from RData files created in previous chapters. These data objects will be used for diversity and abundance analysis comparing samples with low and high environmental diversity. 11.17 Data preparation Note: Exclude outlier sample EHI01340 from all datasets. Transform Hill diversity data from long to wide format and join with sample metadata. Choose a Hill diversity metric (default: h1, exponential Shannon) to split samples into tertiles. Filter to keep only Low and High groups (excluding Mid) for two-group comparisons. Ensure sample metadata and genome count matrices are aligned, keeping only samples present in both datasets and genomes with at least one non-zero count. # --- Configuration: outlier sample to exclude ------------------------------ outlier_sample <- "EHI01340" # Check if outlier sample exists (may already be excluded in previous chapters) if (!outlier_sample %in% sample_metadata$sample) { message("Note: Outlier sample '", outlier_sample, "' not found in sample_metadata (likely already excluded in previous chapters).") } # drop the outlier sample everywhere (safe even if already excluded) sample_metadata <- sample_metadata %>% filter(sample != outlier_sample) # Optimized: Filter genome counts in one pass - select valid samples and filter zero rows valid_sample_cols <- intersect(sample_metadata$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_sample_cols)) %>% filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Validate filtering results if (nrow(sample_metadata) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after filtering. Check sample_metadata.") } if (nrow(genome_counts_filt) == 0) { stop("Error: No genomes remaining after filtering. Check genome_counts_filt.") } # --- choose which Hill order to split on ---------------------------------- # use "h1" by default (exp-Shannon). Change to "h0" or "h2" if you prefer. q_choice <- "h1" # Validate q_choice format valid_q_choices <- c("h0", "h1", "h2") if (!q_choice %in% valid_q_choices) { stop("Error: q_choice must be one of: ", paste(valid_q_choices, collapse = ", ")) } # Validate hill_long exists and has data if (!exists("hill_long") || nrow(hill_long) == 0) { stop("Error: hill_long is missing or empty.") } # Optimized: Build Hill-wide and join with metadata in one pipeline hill_col <- paste0("env_hill_", q_choice) hill_wide <- hill_long %>% filter(id != outlier_sample) %>% rename(sample = id) %>% pivot_wider(id_cols = sample, names_from = q, values_from = value, names_glue = "env_hill_{q}") # Validate pivot_wider results if (!hill_col %in% colnames(hill_wide)) { stop("Error: Hill diversity column '", hill_col, "' not found after pivot_wider. ", "Available columns: ", paste(colnames(hill_wide), collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Join and filter missing Hill data in one step meta_hill <- sample_metadata %>% left_join(hill_wide, by = "sample") %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[hill_col]])) # Remove samples with missing Hill diversity data # Report if any samples were excluded n_excluded_hill <- nrow(sample_metadata) - nrow(meta_hill) if (n_excluded_hill > 0) { warning("Found ", n_excluded_hill, " samples with missing Hill diversity data. These were excluded.") } # Validate we have enough samples for tertiles (need at least 3) if (nrow(meta_hill) < 3) { stop("Error: Insufficient samples (", nrow(meta_hill), ") for creating tertiles. Need at least 3 samples.") } group_col <- paste0("env_group_q", substr(q_choice, 2, 2)) # env_group_q1, etc. # tertiles → keep only Low/High (drop Mid) and fix factor order Low < High # Use tryCatch to handle edge cases in cut_number meta_hill <- tryCatch({ meta_hill %>% mutate( !!group_col := ggplot2::cut_number(.data[[hill_col]], 3, labels = c("Low","Mid","High")) ) %>% filter(.data[[group_col]] %in% c("Low","High")) %>% mutate(!!group_col := factor(.data[[group_col]], levels = c("Low","High"))) }, error = function(e) { stop("Error creating tertiles with cut_number: ", e$message, ". This may occur if there are too few unique values in ", hill_col) }) # Validate group creation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after filtering to Low/High groups.") } # Validate group creation group_counts <- table(meta_hill[[group_col]], useNA = "no") if (any(group_counts == 0)) { stop("Error: One or both groups (Low/High) are empty after filtering. ", paste(names(group_counts), group_counts, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")) } # Optimized: Keep only samples present in both datasets in one pass valid_samples <- intersect(meta_hill$sample, colnames(genome_counts_filt)) if (length(valid_samples) == 0) { stop("Error: No overlapping samples between meta_hill and genome_counts_filt.") } # Filter both datasets to valid samples meta_hill <- meta_hill %>% filter(sample %in% valid_samples) genome_counts_filt <- genome_counts_filt %>% select(genome, all_of(valid_samples)) %>% # Re-filter genomes to ensure they're still present after sample filtering filter(rowSums(across(-genome, ~ .x != 0), na.rm = TRUE) > 0) # Final validation if (nrow(meta_hill) == 0) { stop("Error: No samples remaining after final filtering.") } cat("N Low / High = ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "Low"), " / ", sum(meta_hill[[group_col]] == "High"), "\n", sep = "") ## N Low / High = 25 / 17 11.18 Structural zeros analysis Note: Identify structural zeros - genomes that are completely absent (zero counts) in one group (Low or High) but present in the other. For each genome, determine if it is absent in all Low samples or all High samples, and calculate group means for genomes present in only one group. Create a barplot visualization showing the top 30 genomes by absolute mean difference, with negative values indicating presence only in Low group and positive values indicating presence only in High group.
